content.content:
## The brief, which replaced the shared prefix

Until batch 10 every brief opened with one shared prefix of 47K characters, on the premise that the agents shared its cache. They did not: across agents the prompt cache serves the system prompt and tools, and the first message only when the whole prompt is identical (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "The Workflow tool").

Every brief now opens with a head of about 4K characters:

- the batch's intro;
- the pointer to the `fortress-repo` skill for how to work: set up a call, build, run the old code beside the new, write and run tests, wait, stop processes, commit and report; and the part on how revived Fortress differs, read whole before work, which its `SKILL.md` says every task needs, described and not named, since the scenario checker refuses a brief that names a path under `.claude/skills/` ("No skill text"; `tools/workflow-scenarios.js`). In climb batch 25, with the head naming no part, 9 of the 20 agents read it, against 20 reads in 18 agents at climb batch 24 (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 8);
- the batch table, one line per rung;
- the base build and how the old code runs from it;
- the points to report;
- how to cite: the tree at `file:line`, a FACTS or POSITIONS entry by its bold title, a result by two to five quoted lines and the command;
- where the agent's scratch goes: under the `tmp/` of the worktree its role works in, in the folder its role names or one named for its role, never in the session's scratchpad ("What a batch commits");
- what to do after a compaction: re-read the brief, the first message of the agent's own transcript, and the files it wrote; the coordinator's boot is not the agent's;
- two rules beside the skill: each part of the skill opened in a call of its own, since a call's output past 30,000 characters is saved to a file under a 2K preview and takes another call to read (17 results of climb batch 26, most of them several parts in one `cat`); and each `wait_for` call sent alone in its message, since calls sent together hold the turn until the last returns: climb batch 26's gate sent two, went 481 s without a request, past an agent's five-minute prompt cache, and wrote 94K again (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding s 2 and 4).

The role's own part follows. It says what the role does in this batch and where, and points to the skill's parts by name for the how. Where brief and skill differ, the brief says so and holds.

A long step a brief starts in the background (the rung's distance after, the gate's distance stage, the commit stage's microGPT walk check, the gather's build, harness runs, demos and specification build on the merged tree) is written in the literal form of the skill's `session.md`, "Long commands": `nohup bash -c '( COMMAND ) > LOG 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> LOG' >/dev/null 2>&1 &`, waited for with `wait_for`, called again in a call of its own, sent alone in its message, until it prints `EXIT=`. In climb batch 25 the gather, whose brief named no way to wait, waited twice for 600 s in the foreground on the demos, and each next call wrote its whole context again, 708K, 11.7 % of the run's writes (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 1). No brief names `run_bg`: the session's automatic permission check refused it at all nine of its uses in climb batch 11, in eight agents, since it cannot read the command the function passes to `bash -c`, and the literal form passed (`reviews/batch-11-review.md`, section 3).

The worker reads its rung's whole briefing as its second step, each part in a call of its own: climb batch 26's rung S printed parts 2 and 3 in one call, 32.9K, which the tool saved to a file, and read them only by `grep` (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 4). The skeptic, a judge and a repair round read the `checks` sub-list. A repair on the merged tree reads the `checks` of the rungs its ruling names, and none where it names none.

A rung worker makes its own worktree: nobody makes one at the launch. The brief gives the one command, `seed-worktree.sh <base build> <worktree> <branch> <base>`. It reuses a worktree that exists and a branch already pushed, otherwise cuts the branch from the base, and seeds the build and caches in about 3 s. If it exits 2, the worker builds as `worktrees.md` says and reports it.

## Rung worker

The order of work: seed the worktree; read the briefing; the test first (`tests-writing.md`, "The order"); where the fix belongs, with every way listed; the edit and the build it needs; whole suites only as `tests-running.md` says; the count and distance stages where the section asks and the edit can move them; the three homes of every defect (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded"); competing declarations; the change's own ladder subset (`gate.md`, "The ladder regression"); the specification's text in the S1 form, with every sentence the change makes false listed.

- The test and the fix may share a commit; the order is read in the transcript (P-102, "Test first, the test kept.").
- A new ledger row goes in `record.md` in `ledger.py`'s row template, numbered `NEW-<rung>-<n>` and cited so in tests and reports. The worker never runs `ledger.py add`, `note`, `rewrite` or `close`: `add` numbers a row max + 1, so two branches that each add a row would collide (`gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, D7). The gather numbers them. A note it gives only where the row with it stays within `ledger.py`'s limits (notes 700 characters, the row 1,200), else the row's whole new line, and it lints each row line it gives with `ledger.py check --rows`, which writes nothing: in climb batch 26 six row writes were refused for length at the gather (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 6).
- `record.md` carries, as complete findings, the FACTS entry the rung earns, its ledger notes, the whole new line of each row whose claim its change alters, its new rows, the handover line, and a "Revival change" section, or "Revival change: none" with the reason. The section is material for the skill writer, not skill text, in two labelled parts: "The change", as evidence (the team's source and what it says or does, with `file:line`; what the tree now does, with its test; the reason, as a passage, a checker refusal or a measured failure), and "Provenance" (the question or item, the answer or default it follows, the batch). The worker is told: "Name no question, item, batch, rung or record file in the change, and give no decision's status there; provenance goes in its own part." (the `coordinator` skill's `references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"; `reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "Proposed fix to the mechanism", item 2.)
- `REPORT.md` opens with five provenance lines: problem, spec, precedent, deviation, historical. The `historical:` line names every file of the 2012 tree the rung edits, for the commit message (the protocol's hard rule on the gate).
- The worker does not edit FACTS, the ledger, PLAN, POSITIONS, INDEX, the handover, the tools or `.claude/`: the gather folds `record.md` into them, since every rung would conflict there.
- It commits and pushes its own files on its branch as it goes, so a dead container loses nothing.
- A resume after a kill runs it again from its start with the same brief, which no retry's head reaches (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "Interrupts and process stops"). So step 1 of the brief says that the commits past the base, or in a resume or repair round those after the one that carries the judge's ruling, and the uncommitted edits are its earlier launch's; that the head it reached is the newest of those commits; and where that launch's transcript is, with any extract of it under the worktree's `tmp/`. In climb batch 23 both resumed workers found their predecessors' transcripts on their own and wrote their extracts in the session's scratchpad, and rung W ran its tests on the base's code again (`reviews/batch-23-review.md`, findings 2 and 4).
- It writes `REPORT.md`, `record.md` and a decision record through a Bash heredoc or a script, not the `Write` tool: in climb batch 24 the harness refused the `Write` of `REPORT.md` to four of the seven workers, 'Subagents should return findings as text, not write report files.', and none of the three that wrote it through a heredoc (`reviews/batch-24-review.md`, finding 5).
- Its result carries `reportText` and `recordText` word for word, since the harness often refuses a worker's write of those files; `decisions`, each with the ways not taken, which its skeptic weighs its fixes against; `pointsReached`; and `forCurator`, its questions for the curator.
- A point to report is listed with its evidence, and the rung lands. Only a step that cannot be undone or acts against a decision on record is not taken: the worker stops and says which (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs").

A result of the base's code that the section or briefing gives, a planner's probe among them, is the worker's before, as the landed tables are a stage's: the worker runs that probe on its code only. In climb batch 25 rung C ran the planner's code-generator probe on the base again for a comparison in one session, which a count of refusals does not need (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 6). Its `REPORT.md` names the commit each stage ran on, and says so where a change of code followed the stage's start: climb batch 26's rung T ran its count one code commit before its last and called the table its final tree's (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 8).

A rung that edits only prose has no test and no failure to see. Its text is checked against the tree and the decisions on record. A `testIsStage` rung's test is the checker count or distance stage, run once after its edit and rebuild, its before the last landed gate's table. A rung that changes the compiled checker also times the count stage on the base build before its edit and on its tree once the change is correct, in one session, then makes the second pass that the skill's `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", asks for, which makes the checker faster and keeps its results the same; the brief says that section holds where the brief differs (P-148, "The checker's speed comes right after its correctness.").

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# brief.py RUN_DIR: per agent, the calls that print its briefing (facts-extract.sh with 4 or more record keys, its --part continuations),
# the first one's call index, assistant-message index and seconds after start, the parts read, and the results' chars and estimated tokens (0.40 a char + 110 a call)
import json, os, re, sys, glob
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
from calls import calls
KEY=re.compile(r'"(?:P-\d+|F-\d+|ledger:\d+|doc:[^"]+|code:[^"]+|map:[^"]+)"')
tot=0
for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(sys.argv[1],'agent-*.jsonl'))):
    lab=json.load(open(f[:-6]+'.meta.json')).get('description','')
    cs=calls(f)
    # first message: does the brief hold a briefing command?
    first=open(f).read(400000)
    hasb = 'Your briefing' in first or 'briefing' in first
    bc=[]
    for d in cs:
        inp=d['input'] if isinstance(d['input'],dict) else {}
        cmd=inp.get('command','') or ''

\end{enumerate}

\Library\ declare none of the constant traits.
An expression composed only of numerals and operators is folded, before the
static check and on both implementations, into a \emph{signed constant}, which
holds its value exactly and whose kind its operands give: computed from
numerals without a radix point and without a quotient, it is an integer,
written as an integer numeral or a negated one; computed from numerals without
a radix point with a quotient among its operations, it is a quotient, written as
the reduced quotient of two integer numerals; and computed from a numeral with a
radix point, it is written as a numeral with a radix point, or a negated one,
where its denominator divides a power of ten, and otherwise as the reduced
quotient of two numerals whose numerator has a radix point.
Where nothing fixes the type of a signed constant (\secref{literals}), an
integer takes the default of an integer numeral, a quotient the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and a constant computed from a numeral with a radix point the
type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, whatever its value, so that \EXP{6/3} is a
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{0.5 + 0.5} an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; where a place fixes
a type, the constant is converted into it as a numeral is, with at most one
rounding.
So \EXP{2147483647 + 1} is the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} \EXP{2147483648},
\EXP{-2147483648} is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{x = 7/2} binds the
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} \EXP{7/2}, and \EXP{0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3} is \VAR{true}.
----

opr MINNUM(self, other:QQ):QQ
    opr MAXNUM(self, other:QQ):QQ
end

(** A numeral's own type (\secref{literals}).  Its four numbers are the
    digit count %digits%, the digits after the radix point %fractionDigits%,
    the radix %radix%, and the digits read as one integer in that radix,
    %digitValue%.  A numeral type is written only as a parameter type. **)
trait Numeral extends Number comprises { NaturalNumeral, RadixPointNumeral }
    abstract getter digits(): ZZ32
    abstract getter fractionDigits(): ZZ32
    abstract getter radix(): ZZ32
    abstract getter digitValue(): ZZ
end

(** A numeral without a radix point. **)
value object NaturalNumeral(digits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ) extends Numeral
    getter fractionDigits(): ZZ32
    (** The numeral as the Working Draft writes one: its digits in its radix,
        and %_r% where the radix %r% is not ten. **)
    getter asString(): String
    (** The value as a float, by one rounding. **)
    asFloat(self): RR64
    opr =(self, b:RR64):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:QQ):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:ZZ):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:ZZ64):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:NN64):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:ZZ32):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:NN32):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:RR32):Boolean
end

(** A numeral with a radix point. **)
value object RadixPointNumeral(digits: ZZ32, fractionDigits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ) extends Numeral
    (** The numeral as the Working Draft writes one, with the radix point
        after %digits - fractionDigits% of its digits. **)
    getter asString(): String
    (** The value as a float, by one rounding. **)
    asFloat(self): RR64
    opr =(self, b:RR64):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:QQ):Boolean
    opr =(self, b:RR32):Boolean
end

    coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)

A numeral is converted where it stands, into the type that its place fixes,
and not before, because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect numerals to be polymorphic.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number

be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

content.content:
7:The design is one rule: a numeral converts where it stands, into the declared type, else into the machine default. Six cases get two answers or none; each has a repair.
9:- Undefined: what "fixes a type". Point 1 lists `Any`; the fork review adds `Object`, `Number` and an unbounded `T` (§1.1); the prototype defaulted at all (probe §1, step 2). Repair: a place fixes a type when its declared type declares a coercion from the numeral type (the eight number types; a program's type by point 4) or is a numeral type; every other type, and no type, takes the default. Then `f(3)` at `Number` is a `ZZ32`, and a tuple at `Any` defaults element by element.
10:- Two answers: "by its value" where the value is unknown. Row 946 shows it: a variable of numeral type reads `ZZ32` whatever its value. Inside `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, `t = x` is such an expression; so is a `nat` used as a value, whose value a template does not know (probe §8). Repair: the default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of numeral type; a `nat` used as a value has the type the Draft gives, `NN32` (`trait-parameters.tex:84-86`), or `ZZ32` (P-40), chosen once.
11:- Two answers: the fold against the fields. Point 4 reads the written numeral's four numbers; point 5 folds `7/2`, `-3` and `0.1 + 0.2` into "one numeral", which has no written form: the prototype made `1/3` a radix-3 numeral (probe §1, step 3), and a negative result has no `nat v`. Repair: the fold yields a constant with a sign, as the Draft's `IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]` has one (`constant.tex:49-52`): an integer constant defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient to `QQ`, one with a radix point to `RR64`; a program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only.
12:- Two answers: a static argument that several numerals fix. `<|3000000000, 0.5|>` is a `List[\RR64\]` if each numeral converts exactly into one instantiation, refused if each defaults first (`ZZ64` into `RR64` is written, P-74); an `if` join likewise. Repair: the narrowest default holding every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each converting into it exactly: the tie rule's form (`inference.tex:313-317`).
13:- Two answers: a program's type with no coercion from the numeral type. The prototype chained default and own coercion (probe §10, decision 3); the Draft says coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:407-408`). Repair: refuse, or name the chain as the one exception.
14:- Undefined: "once per class, at load" as a semantics. For a reference object two evaluations of `c: CC64 = 3` become one object, which `SEQV` sees (`objects.tex:51-53`), and a raising coercion fails at load. Repair: a numeral at a program's type denotes one object, as a string literal does (P-171), or hoist value types only.

content.content:
judge (contested) for N, rung-numeral-types stands
I upheld 953d050966; nothing is reverted. The record decides this the skeptic's way. Fork N7, the batch's default for walk's places (explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-29.md:355), names the declared return type as one of the checker's places. It says a numeral there converts from its exact value, that one out of range is "refused at the place when it runs", that a program's type takes it through its coercion from the numeral type, and "else refused". The rung's section repeats the rule: "A numeral out of range at a typed place raises there when it runs" (CLIMB-BATCH-29.md:428). P-173 says walk converts "at the same places, place by place", where the checker refuses a numeral out of range statically (POSITIONS.md:104). P-174 says "A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral" (POSITIONS.md:105). The specification treats "body expressions of functionals and constructors where the return types are declared" as a coercion context, alongside declared variables and parameters (Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:118-127). So a declared return type is a place that fixes a type, and P-173's default does not apply there.

Walk's other typed places already behave this way: they refuse what does not convert and let a coercion's exception through. This holds at the binding (LHSEvaluator.java:221-227, and :235-237, which rethrows), the parameter (NonPrimitive.java:256-270) and the assignment (BaseEnv.java:313-327). The worker's own NumeralOutOfRangeWalk and NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk assert at a binding the same refusals the fix's tests assert at a return.

Worker right: walk checks no return type of a value in general (FunctionClosure.java:209-221), and a return with no declared type takes the default. The fix keeps both: a value that hold
forCurator: []

judge (contested) for T, rung-literals-spec stands
The skeptic's fix 1184add1d9 is upheld. The specification decides the case, and no decision on record changes what it says.

Which sources settle it:
- The Working Draft says "The expression e ≠ e' is semantically equivalent to the expression ¬(e = e')" (Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:272-273; Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262).
- operator-NE says "The infix operator ≠ applies ¬ to the result of = on the same operands" (Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:46-47).
- Each number type points to operator-NE (basic-integers.tex:668; numbers.tex:404).
- The rung's own numbers.tex:51-54 makes u = 0 true at all eight types, through the = pairs that P-173 keeps. With operator-NE standing, the text must therefore give u ≠ 0 false.
- P-173 says only where a numeral converts (Any takes the default). It says nothing of ≠, and neither do P-165, P-168 or P-174.
- So the true answer comes from one library declaration, opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any) = NOT (a=b) at Library/FortressLibrary.fss:98. It defaults the numeral before it applies =, so it does not apply = "on the same operands". That is a departure of the library, not the design's answer.
- Calling it the design's answer is a sentence the decided design does not state, which is the section's one reserved point. The worker listed it as such itself (REPORT.md, "Points to report").

Why the skeptic's form is right:
